messages.message:
The confidence level the limit is quoted at.
The five non-round values are the central-normal probabilities for 1σ through 5σ (68.27%, 95.45%, 99.73%, 99.9937%, 99.999943%), but they are applied here as one-sided confidence levels. A "1σ" choice is therefore not a one-sigma one-sided bound - these are offered because they are familiar numbers, not because the limit is a multiple of any sigma.

Where the knowledge of the background under the peak comes from - and so what you are asserting. This is a separate question from which measurement the limit describes; see the measurement option.
Floating: the continuum is inferred from the same channels that might contain the signal, so nothing is assumed about the neighbourhood. A broad or uniform excess is absorbed into the continuum, so only genuinely peak-shaped excess counts as signal - this is the stricter test of "is that actually a peak?". The default, and the best validated.
Anchored by side channels: the background is measured in the channels beside the region and carried in, which asserts those shoulders contain no signal and that the continuum runs straight through them. A region simply sitting higher than its shoulders now counts as signal, whether or not it is peak-shaped. Requires a linear continuum: four-plus-four side channels barely determine an offset and a slope.
Anchoring adds information, so it usually gives a narrower limit - but a narrower number is not automatically a better one. Floating errs toward wider limits; anchoring errs toward wrong limits, in either direction, if a neighbouring line, a step, or curvature makes the shoulders unrepresentative. Default to Floating, and use the side channels when the region is clean for several FWHM either side and the extra sensitivity is worth the assertion.
Note the shoulders' own counting uncertainty is carried in the likelihood, so a weak anchor honestly widens the limit rather than pretending the continuum is known.

Which measurement the limit is a statement about.
Current spectrum: how much signal could be hiding in the spectrum you have. The ordinary case.
Background reference: the loaded spectrum is asserted to contain no signal, and is used to predict what a future measurement would be able to detect. The reference counts and the projected measurement are scored together, sharing one continuum, so the reference's own counting statistics are carried into the answer rather than wished away.
A background-reference result is a predicted sensitivity, not a bound on the spectrum in hand, and is reported as such. It is a median expectation: there is no future measurement to observe, so the prediction is made at the expected counts.

Asserts this spectrum contains no signal, and uses it to predict what a future measurement could detect.
The result is a predicted sensitivity for a measurement of the planned time, not an upper limit on this spectrum. The reference's own counting statistics are carried into the answer, so a short background gives a correspondingly weaker prediction.

Which quantity to report. These are different products and they use different thresholds on the statistic, so the choice is explicit rather than guessed.
Upper limit: a one-sided bound - "the activity is less than U at this confidence". What is wanted almost always.
Central interval: a two-sided interval - "the activity is between L and U at this confidence".
Note the two roots found at a one-sided threshold do not form a central interval: together they cover only about 2×CL−1, so two 95% one-sided bounds make roughly a 90% central interval. When that happens the result says so rather than calling it an interval.
On a spectrum with no signal a central interval usually runs into the physical boundary at zero, so only the upper endpoint exists; it is then reported as "between 0 and U". That is not the same as a one-sided upper limit at the same confidence - the endpoint sits at a higher threshold, making it a (1+CL)/2 one-sided bound.

The dwell you are asking about. One control, but it reaches the calculation two different ways:
For the Currie method, and when the limit describes the loaded spectrum, the spectrum's channel counts are projected to this real time (and the live time by the same ratio, so the dead-time fraction is preserved).
When the spectrum is a background reference, the reference counts are left alone and this becomes the exposure of the future measurement being predicted - so the reference's own counting statistics are carried into the answer instead of being wished away.
Projecting the spectrum is most accurate for a shorter or comparable dwell; for a much longer one the result is optimistic, since the rate-estimate uncertainty then exceeds the projected Poisson noise. The background-reference route does not have that problem.
Invalid measurement time - expected something like '5 min', '300 s', or '00:05:00'.
Less than {1} at {2} CL (one-sided upper limit), χ2={3}
Predicted sensitivity: less than {1} at {2} CL for a {3} measurement, χ2={4}
Between {1} and {2} at {3} central CL, χ2={4}
Between 0 and {1} at {2} central CL, χ2={3}
Two one-sided {1} bounds: {2} to {3} (~{4} central coverage), χ2={5}
Distance ≥{1} at {2} CL (one-sided lower limit), χ2={3}
χ2 is {1} at large distance, {2} DOF

The quantity labelled χ2 here is the {1} statistic - a Poisson deviance, 2·∑(E − n + n·ln(n/E)), summed once per channel (Cash 1979). It is used instead of a Gaussian χ2 because it has no modified-Neyman variance bias and needs no variance floor for empty channels.
Only differences of it between trial activities are meaningful; a difference follows the same asymptotic χ2 law a Gaussian one would, which is what sets the confidence threshold. Its absolute value does not test goodness of fit: E[statistic] is not (channels − parameters), so a χ2/DOF formed from the two numbers displayed beside each other is not a goodness-of-fit measure and should not be read as one.

The saved state used the retired "assume no signal is present" continuum option. That option asserted the spectrum contains no signal and then ignored the uncertainty of that assertion, which measured about 40% coverage where 95% was claimed. It has been reloaded as a floating continuum on a background-reference measurement, which is what it was reaching for. The measurement time now means the dwell of the future measurement being predicted, rather than a rescaling of this spectrum - check it before relying on the number.
